# Notes Written Before Anyone Commissions a Campaign

*Deliberately before. The moment this becomes a destination-branding exercise, the question stops being "what does this place actually need in order to survive being wanted" and becomes "which agency has the better film," and we will buy the best film, and the film is not the place.*

---

## The sentence in the brief I'd want pulled apart

"Attract more international visitors, sustainably, with benefits to local communities and preservation of cultural heritage."

That reads as one goal with three qualifiers. It is closer to one instrument with three constraints, and nobody has said which is the objective and which is the binding limit. If the number the agency is judged on at year-end is *arrivals*, everything after the first comma is decoration, and we all know it by month nine.

So before any of it: **why aren't people coming now?** Three different diseases produce low international volume, and they take opposite treatments.

**An awareness gap.** The place is genuinely unknown. Treatment: reach. This is the only one a tourism agency can fix by itself, which is precisely why it's the diagnosis everyone reaches for.

**A friction gap.** People know, and half of them give up. Visa forms that time out, no way to book a bed without a phone call in a language they don't speak, a flight that arrives at 01:40, no card acceptance past the second town, no idea how to get from the airport to the valley without hiring a driver they can't vet. Treatment: unglamorous plumbing, no photography involved, and it converts demand that already exists rather than manufacturing new demand.

**A product gap.** They come, they look at the famous thing for three hours, and they leave — because there is nothing to do on day two and nowhere good to sleep on night one. Treatment: build the second and third day. This is where nearly all the economic benefit hides, because *revenue is a function of nights, not arrivals*, and the region currently hosts the impact of a visit while the capital city captures its spending.

My suspicion: mostly the third, with the second quietly halving whatever the first achieves, and the first is what gets funded because it's the only one that appears on this agency's org chart.

**So the first artefacts I'd want aren't a strategy or a brand.** Two documents, neither of them exciting:

1. **A leakage map.** Take one hundred units of visitor spend and follow every one until it leaves the region. Who owns the tour operator, where was the package paid for, who owns the hotel, where was the food grown, who employs the driver, where is the profit banked. In most emerging destinations somewhere between half and four fifths never touches the region at all. That fraction, not the arrivals figure, is the honest measure of whether tourism is a development strategy or a rent extracted from a landscape.

2. **A land ownership and pressure map.** Who owns the parcels within twenty minutes of each significant site, and how has that changed in three years. *This is the document that predicts who will be rich in a decade and who will be renting a room in their own village.* Tourism development is, mechanically, a land-value transfer event. Everything sentimental in the brief about "benefiting local communities" is decided here, before a single visitor lands, and almost always by people who are already watching. If the agency has no view on land, it has no view on community benefit, whatever the strategy document says.

---

## The two things being conflated

**Arrivals and value.** They are separate instruments and they can move in opposite directions — indeed the cheapest way to raise arrivals is day-trip coach traffic from the capital, which fills the site to capacity, wears the stone, irritates residents, and leaves roughly the price of a soft drink behind. A destination can be visibly booming and getting poorer per head. I'd want the plan to state its ambition as **visitor-nights and retained spend**, and to be openly indifferent to arrivals — with the awkward implication accepted early: *the recommendation may be fewer visitors, staying much longer, paying more.* That is not an austerity position. It is the only one that satisfies all three constraints simultaneously, and it also happens to be the only aviation-emissions lever a region actually holds. We cannot make the flight cleaner. We can make it carry a fortnight instead of a weekend.

**Preserving culture and performing it.** These diverge fast. The staged version — costume, scheduled dance, gift shop — is what develops by default when demand arrives without a rule, because it is legible and it scales. It also hollows out what the visitor came for within about a decade, and everyone involved can feel it happening and nobody can stop it, because the incentive runs one way. The living version requires something no code of conduct provides: **a community's enforceable right to refuse.** To close a site during a ceremony, to ban photography in a particular place, to cap group size, to withdraw entirely and lose the agency nothing. Protection without a veto is a poster.

Which points at the asymmetry worth building on. A visitor who is *let in on something* — a house, a kitchen, a working practice, a story told by someone whose grandfather is in it — forms an attachment that no landscape generates on its own. Scenery is admired and forgotten; it is also perfectly substitutable, because there is another mountain. **Being hosted is the only part of the offer that cannot be copied by a competing region, and it is the first thing that dies under volume.** So the scarce asset here isn't the view. It's the plausibility of the encounter.

---

## Where I'd actually put the effort

**Price the fragile things, and let the money visibly stay.** Timed entry and a real fee at the two or three sites that are actually under pressure — with the revenue hypothecated, transparently, to that site's conservation and that specific adjacent community. Free-at-the-point-of-use is the most reliable way to destroy a monument ever devised, and unpriced access transfers the entire surplus to whoever sells the bus ticket. The politics of charging are unpleasant for about one season. The politics of a ruined site are permanent.

**Redistribute in space and time before adding capacity.** Crowding is almost never a regional condition; it's one square kilometre between eleven and two, in nine weeks of the year. The same site at six in the morning is a different site, and a good deal of what looks like a carrying-capacity crisis is a scheduling problem that costs nothing to solve — differential pricing by hour, permits released for the shoulder months, the second and third itinerary built and promoted *before* the first one breaks. Load-shifting is embarrassingly cheap next to construction.

**Ownership, not employment.** There is a real difference between a valley that works in tourism and a valley that owns it, and it is decided in the licensing rules. A small-operator lane in the permit system. Caps or graduated tax on non-resident accommodation ownership. Short-term-let regulation drafted *now*, in the quiet, when nobody has an interest to defend — because no city on earth has managed it afterwards, and residential displacement is the point at which residents stop being hosts and start being an opposition.

**Guides, treated as the highest-leverage intervention in the plan.** A well-trained local guide is simultaneously interpretation, crowd control, heritage protection, safety, and roughly a hundred per cent local value retention. And they should hold the pen: the narrative of the place written by the people from it, with standing permission to overrule anything a ministry drafted that reads as sanitised or false. Not translation — authorship. A story told by someone who is in it survives contact with a curious visitor; a script does not.

**The plate.** The single largest available increase in retained spend is usually food — what's served, who grew it, who cooked it, and whether the hotels are importing frozen product because procurement is easier. This is agricultural extension work and a purchasing standard, and it belongs in a tourism plan for the unromantic reason that it moves more money into more households than any marketing line item will.

**Seed the segments that self-select.** Rather than broad-reach campaigns against Instagrammable competitors — a fight we lose on budget and win on nothing — go narrow and early: the specialist trekking, birding, archaeology, textile, diving, culinary and academic channels, and the diaspora, who arrive pre-trusting, spend in the villages, come back, and defend the place unprompted. These visitors stay longer, travel off-season, behave better, and are markedly less fashionable — meaning less likely to evaporate when the algorithm moves on. *A destination whose demand was manufactured by virality has no defence when virality leaves.*

**Bias hard toward reversibility.** I have a high tolerance for experiments and almost none for concrete. Trails, permits, pricing, festivals, pop-up accommodation, a new route — all cheap to try, cheap to unwind, so try many and kill most. The cruise berth, the coastal road, the 400-room resort, the cable car: these are one-way doors, they arrive with impressive projections and a foreign balance sheet, and they permanently reset what kind of place this can be. The test I'd apply to any proposal: *if this turns out to be wrong in six years, what does undoing it cost?* Where that answer is "nothing can be undone," the burden of proof should be brutal, and the fact that the investor is impatient is not evidence.

**And the plumbing.** Water and waste capacity before beds, not after. Payments, signage, a booking path a stranger can complete in one sitting, a way to reach the valley that doesn't require a private car. Nobody wins an award for this and it converts more visitors than the film.

---

## Measurement, which is where this normally dies

I'd retire arrivals as a target immediately. It is the metric that instructs everyone to fill buses, and everything above is an argument for occasionally letting the bus go elsewhere.

Instead: **retained spend per visitor** and **visitor-nights**, from the leakage map, re-run annually; **share of licensed operators and beds under local ownership**, which is the community-benefit question stated properly; **named ecological indicators at named sites** — trail erosion, water abstraction, wildlife counts — published, with a stated capacity per site per hour that the agency is judged for *staying under*; **resident housing cost against resident income**, the earliest visible signal of the failure mode nobody recovers from; and **resident sentiment**, which I'd weight above visitor satisfaction for the simple reason that visitors leave. Residents turn once, slowly, and then never turn back, and every destination that has been ruined by tourism was ruined in exactly that order.

Plus one qualitative practice I'd protect against every efficiency review: **everyone with decision rights spends one day a quarter in the region without a badge — arriving as a visitor arrives, on the public bus, at the busy hour — and one day sitting in the village nearest the most-visited site, listening, unsummarised.** Dashboards launder resentment out of feedback. The resentment is the finding.

---

## Sequencing, and the part I'd rather not announce

**No launch.** No logo, no slogan, no "Visit —" campaign in year one. Demand generated against a supply chain that isn't ready produces a first cohort of visitors whose reviews are permanent, and those reviews will outlive the campaign that summoned them by a decade. Get the product right in one valley and let the place be *discovered*; a destination reported by its visitors is worth several times one announced by its government, for the same reason a brand's own account is always read as advertising.

Months 0–4: the leakage map, the land map, capacity thresholds at the three sites under real pressure, and a hard look at what the best-run comparable region actually did — including, particularly, what it now regrets.

Months 4–12: one valley as the pilot, unannounced, with the rest of the region as a control. Guide training and authorship, timed entry and hypothecated fees at one site, the food procurement standard with a handful of willing hotels, the licensing rules and short-term-let regulation drafted while nobody is watching, the friction work on booking and payments. Measure retained spend, not footfall.

Then the second and third itineraries, then shoulder-season demand-seeding in the specialist channels, and only then — if the numbers still justify it — beds, roads, and reach.

On governance, briefly: I'd resist the inter-ministerial steering committee. It will meet, it will produce a communiqué, and land use will still be decided elsewhere by people who weren't in the room. The lever the agency actually has is that it can own the only dataset everyone else eventually needs — the leakage map, the capacity thresholds, the land change data. Hold that, publish it, be useful, and become difficult to route around. Standing acquired that way tends to outlast the mandate granted by a memo.

The awkward possibility I'd want on the table from the start: **the highest-value work here may not sit in the tourism agency at all.** It may be land regulation, agricultural procurement, water infrastructure and a licensing regime — with the marketing budget cut to a fraction and pointed at six specialist audiences instead of one mass one. And the honest recommendation may include making one or two places *harder* to reach, and asking to be measured on a number that goes down.

That is an uncomfortable conclusion for whoever commissioned the brief. Worth establishing early — before the film gets made — whether we want the answer or the campaign.
